title: Breaking down Chicago style; riffs and Bix with Whiteman
summary: Ashcraft associates the style with tenor, clarinet and trumpet and one-figure riffs, and says Bix absorbed it from McPartland and the Pollack band.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: We've talked about Chicago style without saying specifically how it was different from, well, just anybody's dance music. Because I think you and I seem to feel that it's so familiar we don't have to do that. But have you ever broken it down into elements and say where it's different, how it's different?

Well, I think we've already mentioned the fact that the force and drive is one of the most important aspects of it. It seems to me that it's easiest if you break it into instruments. That we associate it, for instance, with a tenor, clarinet, and trumpet. We don't associate it with piano. Because I don't think there was any particular... There were some exceptions, but generally it wasn't a particularly distinguished piano. With the exception of Steve Brown, who you don't really associate with Chicago necessarily. The basses didn't matter much. Drum is very rarely recorded until the Krupa and Tuff era. I would say probably that the one note thing that I mentioned could be expanded to say one figure, one particular phrase. And I remember that Teschmarker used one that was a... Or something like it. Or associate...
Now, you wouldn't say that the riff was a characteristic of Chicago. It isn't quite that, is it?

No, but particular riffs were where they were very... Well, one example, for example... I mean, one example is that type of phrase that I was just humming. Freeman did it. Still does it. McPartland played it many, many times. And on one occasion, the best recorded example I can think was made by Bix from Monday on in Mississippi Mud with Whiteman.

Well, I'm saying that because he spent the night, darn near all night with us the night before listening to McPartland and the Pollock Band and talking about that and whistling and thinking about it. And later on in a couple of other Whiteman records, particularly the ones where he played with Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey on trumpet. They made some trio stuff. That riff comes back time and time again. But it's because it's a forced riff. It's almost that it's a pile driver effect.
On the beat? Ahead the beat?

It's ahead. Da, Those notes aren't always in it. But I mean, the essence of it is in it. You can feel it in the Pollock Band. And see, Bix had slid through Chicago so fast, really, and had spent so much time with Hoagie and the Poet Monk House in Bloomington, Indiana, and in playing around in there, that he developed this lovely singing style that he developed, but with this underlying softer beat than the Chicagoans later developed. Bix would have been perfectly wonderful in that kind of a Chicago band. But Bix, later on with Goldkett, showed that he knew some of this thing. Bix was not a very loud player, you see, anyway. He never played with a band except Goldkett that ever tried to blow, consciously, to blow the roof off. Well, the Austin boys were consciously trying to blow down the wall. And with Goldkett, which was, for its time, a powerhouse band, you would still find on a thing like Blue Room, where they make the climb up the middle, that Bix would ring out of the top of that with all the wallop of a Chicago band. But at that point, people thought of Chicago band as being loud, imaginative, and very musicianally.
